options.D: The share of staff who signed the code of conduct this year

questions.key_concept: Risk culture shows in behavior, especially whether leaders act when problems are reported, not in counts of training or policies.
questions.pre_read: Ask which option shows how people behave when risk comes to the surface.
questions.correct_explanation: Risk culture is the values and beliefs people share about risk and the behavior they drive, so the best sign is what happens when risk surfaces. The share of reported control failures that managers follow up shows whether raising an issue leads to action, which decides whether staff keep raising them. Course completion is the runner-up: it shows that people sat the training, not whether they speak up or are heard when they do.

wrong_explanations.A: Completion shows attendance, not behavior. Staff can finish the course and still hide problems if raising them is punished.
wrong_explanations.B: A count of approved policies measures paperwork. Culture shows in how people act on risk, which policies alone do not change.
wrong_explanations.D: A signature shows acknowledgment, not conduct. Staff can sign the code and still stay silent about failures.

tips: Eliminate: B and D measure documents and signatures, which show that rules exist, not how people behave around risk.
Final two: C beats A because follow-up of reported failures shows the culture in action, while course completion only shows attendance.
Exam cue: to judge risk culture, look for behavior when risk surfaces, such as reporting and how leaders react, over counts of courses or policies.

questions.subtopic: 1A1 Strategy, goals and objectives. Late IT goal
questions.question: A university's IT department made rollout of a new identity platform its top goal, and the rollout is now four months late. How should the risk practitioner BEST express this risk to senior management?

options.A: As the delay's effect on the goals the platform serves
options.B: As the project milestones the rollout has missed so far
options.C: As the security goals the new platform has not yet reached
options.D: As the budget the rollout has spent against plan

questions.key_concept: Risk to an IT goal is expressed through its effect on the enterprise goals it serves, not through project or technical measures.
questions.pre_read: Ask which description leaders could weigh against risks elsewhere in the enterprise.
questions.correct_explanation: In the COBIT 2019 goals cascade, alignment goals (the IT goals) serve enterprise goals, so a late IT goal matters through what it puts at risk above it, such as student access to systems or research data protection. Expressed that way, senior management can weigh it against other business risks and appetite. Unmet security goals are the runner-up: closer to impact than milestones, but still alignment-level measures until tied to enterprise goals.

wrong_explanations.B: Missed milestones describe project progress. They do not tell leaders what the delay puts at risk for the university.
wrong_explanations.C: Security goals are alignment-level means. Leaders can weigh a shortfall only once it is tied to the enterprise goals it supports.
wrong_explanations.D: Spend against plan is a project measure. Overspending matters, but it says nothing about which business goals the delay threatens.

tips: Eliminate: B and D are project measures of schedule and spend that say nothing about what the delay threatens.
Final two: A beats C because security goals are alignment-level means in the goals cascade; leaders weigh risk through the enterprise goals above them.
Exam cue: when an IT goal or project slips, report it through the enterprise goal it serves, not through milestones or technical targets.

questions.subtopic: 1A6 Organizational asset management. Unrecorded AI training data
questions.question: A retailer's data science team built a three-year sales dataset to train the pricing department's AI model, but it is missing from the asset inventory. What should the risk practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Assess the dataset's exposure where it is stored
options.B: Record the data science team as the business owner
options.C: Encrypt the storage that holds the dataset
options.D: Identify a business owner for the dataset

questions.key_concept: AI training datasets are assets: give each a business owner first, since classification and risk decisions depend on ownership.
questions.pre_read: Sort the options into steps, then find the one the other steps rely on.
questions.correct_explanation: Classification, valuation and risk acceptance all depend on who owns an asset, so the first step for an unrecorded dataset is to identify its business owner, likely in the pricing department the model serves. With an owner, the dataset can be classified, recorded and assessed. Assessing exposure is the runner-up: without an owner to set the data's classification, there is no agreed basis for rating the exposure and no one to decide on it.

wrong_explanations.A: Exposure can be rated once the dataset is classified, and its owner is the one who classifies it and decides on the risk.
wrong_explanations.B: Building a dataset makes the data science team its developer or custodian, not its owner. Ownership sits with the business that relies on it.
wrong_explanations.C: Encryption is a control chosen before the data is classified or its risk analyzed, so it may not fit what the data needs.

tips: Eliminate: B confuses the team that built the dataset with its business owner, and C picks a control before the data is classified or analyzed.
Final two: D beats A because the owner classifies the dataset and decides on its risk; rating the exposure needs that basis first.
Exam cue: for an asset missing from the inventory, AI datasets included, establish the business owner first; classification and risk rating follow.

questions.subtopic: 1B2 Lines of defense. Blocked risk reporting
questions.question: At a retailer, the CRO reports to the CFO, who has twice cut high-rated finance system risks from reports bound for the board. What is the BEST structural change for the risk practitioner to recommend?

options.A: Move the risk function under internal audit
options.B: Give the CRO direct access to the board risk committee
options.C: Have the CFO sign off each report's risk ratings
options.D: Have internal audit vet each report before the board

questions.key_concept: The second line sits within management but needs an escalation route to the board that executives cannot block.
questions.pre_read: Notice who controls the risk function's reporting line today.
questions.correct_explanation: The second line sits within management but needs an escalation route that management cannot block. Direct access from the CRO to the board risk committee lets significant risks reach the board even when a senior executive objects, which removes the cause of the omissions. Having internal audit vet each report is the runner-up: it adds a check, but approving management's reports is a management duty that would weaken audit's independence.

wrong_explanations.A: Placing the risk function under internal audit merges the second and third lines, so audit would be assuring work it runs.
wrong_explanations.C: A CFO sign-off makes official the very filter that removed the risks, giving the CFO more control over what the board sees.
wrong_explanations.D: Vetting management's risk reports is a management duty. Audit would lose independence, and the CRO would still have no route of its own.

tips: Eliminate: A merges the second line into internal audit, and C makes the CFO's filter official instead of removing it.
Final two: B beats D because the second line needs its own escalation route to the board; vetting reports pulls internal audit into management work.
Exam cue: when management can block the second line's reporting, look for a direct escalation path to the board, not another approval step.

questions.subtopic: 1A4 Policies and standards. Procedure change against a standard
questions.question: At a bank, the access control standard requires quarterly access reviews, and the team that owns the review procedure wants to rewrite it to run the reviews yearly. What is the risk practitioner's BEST advice?

options.A: Accept a yearly cycle if the team logs an exception
options.B: Let the procedure's owner set the review frequency
options.C: Approve the yearly cycle as a procedure update
options.D: Refer the change to the standard's owner to decide

questions.key_concept: A procedure carries out a standard and cannot relax it; changing a mandatory requirement is a decision for the standard's owner.
questions.pre_read: Place each document in the policy hierarchy before reading the options.
questions.correct_explanation: A procedure sets out the steps for meeting a standard, so it cannot relax what the standard requires. Moving from quarterly to yearly reviews changes the standard itself, which its owner decides, informed by the practitioner's analysis of what a longer cycle would add to risk. Letting the procedure's owner set the frequency is the runner-up: the team owns its steps, but not the mandatory requirement those steps exist to meet.

wrong_explanations.A: An exception covers a specific, time-limited gap approved by the risk owner. It is not a way to rewrite a requirement, and the practitioner does not accept it.
wrong_explanations.B: Procedure owners control how the steps are done, not the mandatory requirement. A yearly cycle would quietly override the standard.
wrong_explanations.C: Approving a change to a mandatory requirement is not the practitioner's role, and a procedure update cannot relax the standard it carries out.

tips: Eliminate: A uses an exception to make a permanent change, and C has the practitioner approve a change that a procedure cannot make.
Final two: D beats B because procedures must conform to standards; a team can change its steps but not the requirement they meet.
Exam cue: a lower layer of the policy hierarchy cannot override a higher one; a change to a requirement goes to the owner of that layer.

questions.subtopic: 1B1 Enterprise risk management (ERM). Same risk in two categories
questions.question: At a retail group, one unit files card-data theft under technology risk and another under compliance, so the profile splits the exposure. Which of the following should the risk practitioner recommend as the BEST fix?

options.A: Merge the units' entries by hand at each quarterly roll-up
options.B: Have IT own the card-data risks filed under technology
options.C: Report each unit's categories to the board as filed
options.D: Propose one group taxonomy for senior management approval

questions.key_concept: A shared risk taxonomy, approved by senior management, lets units record the same risk the same way so it rolls up whole.
questions.pre_read: Ask why the exposure splits, not only how to repair this one case.
questions.correct_explanation: The exposure splits because units sort the same risk into different categories, so the cause is a missing shared taxonomy. A group taxonomy, approved by senior management as part of the risk framework, lets every unit file the risk the same way and the profile show its full size. Merging entries by hand is the runner-up: it repairs this one risk at each roll-up but leaves the cause, and the next mismatch, in place.

wrong_explanations.A: A manual merge treats the symptom. Each roll-up depends on someone spotting mismatches, and other risks split the same way go unnoticed.
wrong_explanations.B: Ownership follows the affected objective, not a category label. Card-data theft hits business and compliance objectives, so IT is not its natural owner.
wrong_explanations.C: Reporting categories as filed passes the split to the board, which then sees the exposure understated in each category.

tips: Eliminate: B lets a category label decide ownership, and C passes the inconsistent categories straight to the board.
Final two: D beats A because a shared taxonomy removes the cause of the split; merging by hand repairs it one roll-up at a time.
Exam cue: when units' risks cannot be combined or compared, look for a common taxonomy or scale approved by senior management.

questions.subtopic: 1A2 Organizational structure, roles and responsibilities. Two accountable names
questions.question: A university's RACI chart lists both the CIO and the registrar as accountable for the risk of exam results being released in error. What is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Keep the CIO and the registrar jointly accountable
options.B: Name the registrar accountable and the CIO responsible
options.C: Name the CIO accountable and the registrar consulted
options.D: Make the academic board accountable for the risk

questions.key_concept: A RACI chart has one accountable person per activity: the business manager whose objective is at risk, with IT responsible.
questions.pre_read: Recall how many people a RACI chart allows to be accountable for one activity.
questions.correct_explanation: A RACI chart has one accountable person per activity, and accountability for a risk sits with the business manager whose objective it affects. Releasing correct results is the registrar's objective, so the registrar is accountable, while the CIO is responsible for the system controls that support it. Making the CIO accountable is the runner-up: IT runs the platform, but running a system does not make IT the owner of the business risk.

wrong_explanations.A: Joint accountability blurs who decides. When two people are accountable, each can assume the other will act.
wrong_explanations.C: The CIO runs the platform but does not own the outcome. The risk falls on the registrar's objective of releasing correct results.
wrong_explanations.D: A board or committee oversees but cannot be the single accountable person. Accountability needs one named manager with authority.

tips: Eliminate: A keeps two accountable people, and D gives accountability to a body; a RACI chart needs one named accountable person.
Final two: B beats C because the risk hits the registrar's objective; the CIO is responsible for the platform's controls, not accountable for the outcome.
Exam cue: one activity, one accountable person, and it is the business manager whose objective is at risk; IT is usually responsible.

questions.subtopic: 1A5 Business processes and resilience. Process spanning three teams
questions.question: An online pharmacy's order fulfillment runs through customer service, IT and the warehouse, and each team's continuity plan covers only its own steps. What should the risk practitioner recommend as the BEST improvement?

options.A: Have IT merge the three plans into one document
options.B: Test the fulfillment teams' plans together each year
options.C: Have each team's plan owner review the other plans
options.D: Name one owner for the end-to-end fulfillment process

questions.key_concept: A critical process that spans teams needs one end-to-end owner accountable for its recovery needs and plans.
questions.pre_read: Compare what each option changes: the plans, the testing or how the process is run.
questions.correct_explanation: Each team plans for its own steps, so no one answers for orders getting through from end to end, and gaps at the handoffs go unowned. Naming one process owner gives fulfillment someone accountable for its recovery needs and for a plan that joins the steps up. A joint test is the runner-up: it could expose handoff gaps, but without a process owner no one is accountable for setting the requirement or closing them.

wrong_explanations.A: Merging documents is clerical work by IT. A single file with no process owner still leaves the handoffs between teams unowned.
wrong_explanations.B: A joint test may reveal gaps, but someone must own the process to set recovery needs and fix what the test finds.
wrong_explanations.C: Peer review spreads the work across the same three silos. It adds checks but no one accountable for the whole process.

tips: Eliminate: A treats the gap as a document task for IT, and C keeps three separate plan owners checking one another.
Final two: D beats B because a test can only find gaps; a process owner is needed to set recovery needs and close them.
Exam cue: when a critical process spans teams and each plans alone, look for one accountable process owner before more testing or paperwork.

questions.subtopic: 1B4 Risk appetite and risk tolerance. Appetite for AI uses
questions.question: An insurer's board has a low appetite for harm to policyholders, and units want generative AI in claims and customer service. Which of the following should the risk practitioner propose to BEST apply that appetite?

options.A: Allowed, review-needed and prohibited tiers of AI use
options.B: A minimum accuracy level for each AI model in use
options.C: A ban on customer-facing AI until regulators publish rules
options.D: CISO approval of each AI use case before launch

questions.key_concept: AI appetite becomes usable when it sorts uses into allowed, review-needed and prohibited tiers that owners can apply.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a business owner would need in hand when the next AI request arrives.
questions.correct_explanation: A broad appetite statement guides AI decisions once it says which uses fit. Tiers of allowed, review-needed and prohibited uses turn a low appetite for harm to policyholders into a rule owners can apply to each new use case, with closer review where harm is likelier. A minimum accuracy level is the runner-up: it is measurable, but accuracy is one property of a model and says nothing about which uses the insurer will accept.

wrong_explanations.B: Accuracy is one measure of a model, not an expression of appetite. A highly accurate model can still be used where harm is unacceptable.
wrong_explanations.C: Low appetite is not zero appetite. A ban chooses avoidance for every use before its risk is analyzed, including low-harm uses.
wrong_explanations.D: The CISO covers security, while decisions on harm to policyholders sit with business owners within the board's appetite. One technical approver does not express appetite.

tips: Eliminate: C treats low appetite as zero and bans every use, and D gives decisions on harm to policyholders to a security approver.
Final two: A beats B because tiers say which AI uses the insurer accepts; an accuracy level measures a model, not the insurer's appetite for harm.
Exam cue: to make appetite usable, look for statements that tell owners which activities fit, need extra review or are out of bounds.

questions.subtopic: 1A3 Organizational culture and ethics. Praise for a skipped review
questions.question: A fintech's CEO publicly praised a team that launched by skipping the required security review, and two more teams plan to skip it. What is the risk practitioner's MOST effective recommendation to stop the trend?

options.A: Retrain product teams on the security review process
options.B: Ask the CEO to restate support for the review
options.C: Tighten the security review policy for launches
options.D: Have the security team review the launched product

questions.key_concept: Tone at the top drives behavior: when a leader rewards a skipped control, the fix starts with that leader restating the rule.
questions.pre_read: Look for what is driving the other teams' plans.
questions.correct_explanation: Staff take their cue from what leaders reward, and the CEO's praise told teams that skipping the review pays. The trend stops when the same leader restates that the review is required, which changes the signal at its source. Retraining is the runner-up: the teams already know the review exists, since they plan to skip it, so more training cannot outweigh a public reward from the CEO.

wrong_explanations.A: The teams know the review is required; they plan to skip it anyway. Training cannot outweigh a reward signal from the top.
wrong_explanations.C: A stricter policy restates intent, but the CEO's praise rewarded working around it; teams will keep doing so while that signal stands.
wrong_explanations.D: Reviewing the launched product deals with one product's risk but leaves the signal that is driving the other teams' plans.

tips: Eliminate: C tightens a rule the teams already work around, and D treats one product's risk while the trend continues.
Final two: B beats A because the teams already know the rule; the CEO's praise is the cause, so the fix starts with the same leader.

questions.subtopic: 1B3 Risk profile. Request to send the full register
questions.question: A shipping company's CIO proposes sending the board the full IT risk register of 240 entries in place of the risk profile, so nothing is hidden. What is the risk practitioner's BEST response?

options.A: Send the full register, ranked from highest rating down
options.B: Keep the profile, traceable to the register entries
options.C: Send the register's high-rated entries in its place
options.D: Send the profile and the full register each quarter

questions.key_concept: The board decides from the aggregated risk profile; keeping it traceable to the register answers the worry that detail is hidden.

questions.correct_explanation: The register is the detailed working record; the profile aggregates and prioritizes it into the view leaders need to decide, set against appetite. Sending both documents is the runner-up: it adds 240 entries to every board pack and buries the few decisions the board must make.

wrong_explanations.A: A ranked register of 240 entries is detail for owners and the risk team. The board needs aggregated exposure against appetite to decide.

wrong_explanations.D: Adding the full register to each pack buries the decisions. Traceability lets the board ask for any detail without receiving all of it.

tips: Eliminate: A and C both send register entries, ranked or filtered, which lack the aggregated view against appetite that the board needs.

questions.subtopic: 1A1 Strategy, goals and objectives. Growth goal against a control
questions.question: A bank's director who owns account opening wants two-minute sign-ups for growth, using an automated ID check that meets regulatory rules but misses more forgeries than staff review. What is the risk practitioner's BEST approach?

options.A: Recommend the design that keeps the manual ID check
options.B: Support the two-minute design that the director prefers
options.C: Ask compliance to set the appetite for ID checks
options.D: Give the director each design's risk against appetite

questions.key_concept: When objectives pull against a control, the practitioner analyzes each option's risk against appetite and the owner of the objective decides.
questions.pre_read: Notice who owns the process and which goals are pulling against each other.
questions.correct_explanation: The trade-off between growth and fraud control belongs to the director who owns account opening, within the appetite leaders have set. Both designs meet regulatory rules, so the choice turns on fraud risk: giving the director each design's fraud exposure against appetite lets them choose with the risk in view. Recommending the manual check is the runner-up: it may prove right, but it settles the trade-off before each design's risk is analyzed.

wrong_explanations.A: Keeping the manual check may be the outcome, but recommending it before each design's fraud risk is analyzed decides the trade-off for the owner and may give up growth needlessly.
wrong_explanations.B: Backing the two-minute design favors growth before its fraud risk is known, and the choice is the director's to make.
wrong_explanations.C: Appetite is set by the board and senior management, not by compliance. Compliance is consulted on the obligations a design must meet.

questions.subtopic: 1A6 Organizational asset management. IT named as owner
questions.question: An engineering firm's asset inventory names the IT infrastructure team as owner of the 40 project file shares it administers. Which of the following is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Keep IT as owner of the shares it administers
options.B: Have IT classify each share by its business use
options.C: Name a business owner for each share's data
options.D: Move ownership of the shares to the risk team

questions.key_concept: IT that administers an asset is its custodian; a named business owner answers for it and sets its classification.
questions.pre_read: Separate who looks after an asset day to day from who answers for it.
questions.correct_explanation: IT administers the shares, which makes it the custodian; the owner is the business manager accountable for the data's use and protection, such as each project's director. Naming business owners comes first because classification, valuation and risk acceptance all depend on them. Having IT classify the shares is the runner-up: classification is needed, but the owner sets it, since the business knows what the data is worth and how sensitive it is.

wrong_explanations.A: Administering a share makes IT its custodian. Ownership sits with the business that relies on the data and decides how it is used.
wrong_explanations.B: The owner classifies data, because the business knows its sensitivity and value. IT then applies the protection the class calls for.
wrong_explanations.D: The risk team oversees and challenges; owning assets would make it the first-line manager of what it monitors.

tips: Eliminate: A treats the custodian as the owner, and D gives second-line staff a first-line ownership role.
Final two: C beats B because classification is the owner's call; the business owner must be named before the data can be classified.
Exam cue: IT is usually the custodian; when an inventory names IT as owner, look for the business owner who answers for the data.

questions.subtopic: 1B5 Risk frameworks, legal, regulatory and contractual requirements. Client notice term
questions.question: A payroll software provider has signed a bank client's contract requiring breach notice within 24 hours, but its incident procedure allows 72 hours. What should the risk practitioner recommend as the BEST action?

options.A: Have the procedure's owner meet the 24-hour term
options.B: Ask the bank to accept the 72-hour procedure instead
options.C: Note the gap for the owner's next yearly review
options.D: Rely on cyber insurance to cover late-notice penalties

questions.key_concept: A signed customer contract term is an obligation in force; internal procedures must be aligned so it can be met.
questions.pre_read: Notice whether the contract is proposed or already in force.
questions.correct_explanation: A signed contract term is an obligation the provider has already accepted, so its incident procedure must be able to meet it. Having the procedure's owner bring notice within 24 hours closes the gap before a breach tests it. Asking the bank to accept 72 hours is the runner-up: renegotiation is possible, but the term binds from signing, so any breach handled before a change is agreed would put the provider in default.

wrong_explanations.B: The term binds from signing. Until the bank agrees a change, a breach handled under the 72-hour procedure would breach the contract.
wrong_explanations.C: The obligation applies now. Waiting for a yearly review leaves months in which any breach would be reported late.
wrong_explanations.D: Insurance may cover some costs, but it does not meet the term or protect the client relationship. Accountability stays with the provider.

tips: Eliminate: C waits for a scheduled review while the term already applies, and D treats insurance as if it moved the obligation.
Final two: A beats B because the signed term binds now; aligning the procedure meets it, while renegotiating leaves the gap open meanwhile.
Exam cue: commitments in customer contracts become obligations with owners; close gaps between contract terms and internal procedures.

questions.subtopic: 1A2 Organizational structure, roles and responsibilities. Owner asks the analyst to choose
questions.question: A distributor's operations director, who owns the warehouse robot outage risk, asks the risk analyst to pick whichever of three treatment options the analyst thinks best. What is the analyst's BEST response?

options.A: Choose the option that cuts the risk the most
options.B: Ask the risk committee to choose an option
options.C: Recommend one option with its cost and benefit
options.D: Choose the cheapest option that meets appetite

questions.key_concept: The practitioner recommends with costs and benefits; the risk owner decides the response, even when asked to hand it over.
questions.pre_read: Notice who owns the risk, and who is being asked to decide.
questions.correct_explanation: The owner decides the response, even when they would rather not. The analyst's job is to recommend, so presenting a preferred option with its cost, benefit and resulting risk lets the director make an informed choice and record it. Asking the risk committee to choose is the runner-up: a committee oversees and challenges, but handing it the choice moves the decision away from the director who is accountable for the risk.

wrong_explanations.A: Picking the strongest option makes the analyst the decision-maker and may spend more than the risk warrants. The choice belongs to the owner.
wrong_explanations.B: A committee oversees and may challenge, but choosing the response for an owned risk shifts accountability away from the director.
wrong_explanations.D: Even within appetite, choosing and recording the response is the owner's act. The analyst recommends; the director decides.

tips: Eliminate: A and D have the analyst choose the response, which is the risk owner's decision however the choice is made.
Final two: C beats B because the director owns the risk; the analyst recommends to the owner instead of moving the decision to a committee.
Exam cue: when an owner asks the practitioner to decide, recommend with costs and benefits and leave the decision with the owner.

questions.subtopic: 1B1 Enterprise risk management (ERM). Framework after major change
questions.question: A media group approved its risk management framework four years ago and has since moved most systems to the cloud and bought two firms. What should the risk practitioner check FIRST in reviewing it?

options.A: Whether its rating scales match those of peer media groups
options.B: Whether internal audit has rated the framework effective
options.C: Whether its scope and roles still cover the whole group
options.D: Whether each unit's register uses its current methods

questions.key_concept: After major change, a framework review starts by checking that its scope and roles still cover the enterprise as it now is.
questions.pre_read: Ask which check the rest of the review depends on.
questions.correct_explanation: After major change, the first question is whether the framework still reaches the group as it now is. Cloud services and two acquired firms may sit outside its scope and roles, so checking coverage shows what the revision must add before senior management approves it. Checking how units use its methods is the runner-up: adoption matters, but it can only be judged inside the existing scope, which may leave out the new firms.

wrong_explanations.A: Peer comparison may inform the scales, but it does not show whether the group's own changes are covered.
wrong_explanations.B: An audit rating describes the framework as it was. It does not show whether the new firms and cloud services fall inside it.
wrong_explanations.D: Checking use of the methods tests adoption within the current scope; the acquired firms and cloud services may not be in that scope at all.

tips: Eliminate: A benchmarks against peers and B relies on a past audit rating; neither shows whether the group's changes are covered.
Final two: C beats D because the changes in the stem are about reach; adoption can only be checked inside a scope that may omit the new firms.
Exam cue: after a merger, acquisition or platform shift, check first that the framework's scope and roles reach the changed enterprise.

questions.subtopic: 1A3 Organizational culture and ethics. Request for loss figures
questions.question: An industry peer group asks a bank's risk analyst for the bank's ransomware loss figures to build a sector benchmark. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Share the figures under the group's confidentiality promise
options.B: Share the figures once system names are removed
options.C: Decline to take part in the sector benchmark
options.D: Seek the bank's approval before sharing the figures

questions.key_concept: Information gained at work is released only with the organization's approval or under legal authority, so ask before sharing it.
questions.pre_read: Ask who has the right to decide what happens to the figures.
questions.correct_explanation: The ISACA Code of Professional Ethics asks members to keep information gained in their work confidential and not release it to inappropriate parties. The loss figures belong to the bank, so the first step is to seek approval from whoever can authorize their release, who may agree, set conditions or refuse. Declining is the runner-up: it protects the data, but it makes the bank's decision for it and may give up a useful benchmark.

wrong_explanations.A: A peer group's promise does not authorize release. The figures are the bank's information, and only the bank can decide who receives them.
wrong_explanations.B: Removing system names may reduce harm, but the loss figures are still the bank's confidential information, released without its approval.
wrong_explanations.C: Declining protects the data but decides for the bank, which may choose to share approved figures if the benchmark serves it.

tips: Eliminate: A treats an outsider's promise as permission, and B assumes that removing names makes the bank's data the analyst's to release.
Final two: D beats C because release is the bank's decision; the analyst seeks approval instead of refusing on the bank's behalf.
Exam cue: information gained at work stays confidential unless its owner, or the law, authorizes release; ask before sharing.

questions.subtopic: 1A5 Business processes and resilience. Exercise gap with a planned fix
questions.question: A broadcaster's continuity exercise found its backup studio could not run playout remotely, and the head of playout approved a fix due in six months. How should the risk practitioner BEST record the gap?

options.A: Rate current risk, with the fix as the action plan
options.B: Rate the risk at the level the approved fix will reach
options.C: Close the finding and track the fix as a project
options.D: Leave the risk unrated until the fix is tested

questions.key_concept: A continuity gap is rated at its current level, counting only what is in place; the approved fix is tracked as its action plan.
questions.pre_read: Separate what is in place today from what has only been approved.
questions.correct_explanation: Exercise gaps become register risks with an owner and an action plan. Until the fix is in place, playout still cannot run remotely, so the rating reflects that current exposure against appetite, with the approved fix tracked as the action plan. Rating at the level the fix will reach is the runner-up: that is the target risk, which judges the plan, but reporting it now would hide six months of exposure.

wrong_explanations.B: The level the fix will reach is the target risk. It shows whether the plan is enough; reported as today's rating, it hides the exposure until then.
wrong_explanations.C: An approved fix is a plan, not a control. Closing the finding removes the gap from view while playout still cannot run remotely.
wrong_explanations.D: Leaving the risk unrated keeps a known gap out of the profile for six months. The exercise already gives enough to rate it now.

tips: Eliminate: C closes a gap that still exists, and D leaves a known gap unrated until a test months away.
Final two: A beats B because current risk counts only what is in place; the level the fix will reach is the target, used to judge the plan, not to report today.
Exam cue: an approved fix changes the action plan, not today's rating; rate current risk until the response is implemented.

questions.subtopic: 1A6 Organizational asset management. Tools found at each count
questions.question: Each yearly asset count at an architecture firm finds cloud tools bought on staff expense cards that no one listed. Which of the following is the BEST fix for the risk practitioner to recommend?

options.A: Run the asset count each quarter instead of yearly
options.B: Record new tools at expense and purchase approval
options.C: Have IT scan the network each month for new devices
options.D: Have IT block new cloud sign-ups from company laptops

questions.key_concept: Keep the inventory current by linking it to purchasing and change processes, not by more frequent clean-up counts.
questions.pre_read: Ask how these tools enter the firm without being recorded.
questions.correct_explanation: The tools are missed because they enter through expense claims, a route the inventory process does not watch, so the cause is a process gap. Recording each new tool when its expense or purchase is approved captures it, with an owner, as it arrives. A quarterly count is the runner-up: it finds the tools sooner, but it still relies on clean-up after the fact instead of recording them when they are bought.

wrong_explanations.A: A more frequent count shortens the gap but keeps the same cause. Tools still arrive unrecorded and are found only later.
wrong_explanations.C: Network scans find devices on the firm's network. Cloud subscriptions bought on cards run on the provider's systems and are easily missed.
wrong_explanations.D: Blocking sign-ups stops tools staff may need and is a control chosen before the risk is analyzed; it does not fix how tools are recorded.

tips: Eliminate: C looks for devices when the missing assets are cloud subscriptions, and D blocks tools instead of fixing how they are recorded.
Final two: B beats A because recording tools at purchase removes the cause; counting more often only finds them sooner.
Exam cue: when an inventory keeps missing the same kind of asset, fix the process that lets it in unrecorded, not how often it is counted.

questions.subtopic: 1B2 Lines of defense. Unchallenged self-assessments
questions.question: Business units at an insurer rate their own controls in yearly self-assessments, and the risk team passes the ratings to the board unchanged. What should the risk practitioner recommend as the BEST change?

options.A: Have internal audit check each self-assessment first
options.B: Have business units rate one another's controls
options.C: Have the risk team challenge ratings before reporting them
options.D: Replace the self-assessments with the risk team's ratings

questions.key_concept: The second line reviews and challenges first-line self-assessments before they are reported; internal audit assures independently.
questions.pre_read: Match each option to the line of defense it would put to work.
questions.correct_explanation: Self-assessment by the first line is a sound start, but the second line's job is to review and challenge it before it reaches the board. Having the risk team test the ratings against evidence, and question those that look optimistic, gives the board ratings it can rely on. Having internal audit check each one is the runner-up: audit gives periodic independent assurance, but routine challenge of first-line ratings is second-line work.

wrong_explanations.A: Internal audit assures on a risk-based plan; checking each unit's self-assessment every year does the second line's routine oversight for it.
wrong_explanations.B: Peer rating still leaves first-line managers marking first-line work. It adds no independent oversight or challenge.
wrong_explanations.D: Replacing the units' ratings takes risk and control ownership away from the first line, which must own and assess its own controls.

tips: Eliminate: B keeps the rating inside the first line, and D has the second line take over ratings that the first line owns.
Final two: C beats A because challenging first-line ratings is the second line's routine role; internal audit gives periodic independent assurance.
Exam cue: the first line self-assesses, the second line challenges, the third line assures; match each fix to the line whose job it is.

questions.subtopic: 1A1 Strategy, goals and objectives. Approving AI pilots
questions.question: Several departments at a hotel group want to start generative AI pilots. Which of the following should the risk practitioner propose as the MOST important criterion for approving each pilot?

options.A: The accuracy objective the tool met in vendor tests
options.B: The business savings the vendor projects for it
options.C: The business objective the pilot is meant to serve
options.D: The data science team's capacity to support the pilot

questions.key_concept: AI initiatives start from a business objective, which gives value, risk and ownership something to be judged against.
questions.pre_read: Ask which criterion the other criteria would be measured against.
questions.correct_explanation: AI initiatives start from a business purpose: without a defined objective there is nothing to measure benefit or risk against, and no clear owner. Requiring each pilot to name the objective it serves lets the hotel group judge its value and risk through that objective and assign the manager who owns it. Vendor-projected savings are the runner-up: they look like business value, but they are the vendor's claim, not a goal the group has set.

wrong_explanations.A: Vendor test accuracy describes the tool, not why the group needs it. A precise tool can still serve no goal worth its risk.
wrong_explanations.B: Projected savings are the vendor's estimate, not a business goal. They can be judged only against an objective the group has set.
wrong_explanations.D: Support capacity matters for delivery, but it ranks pilots by what the team can handle, not by what the business needs.

tips: Eliminate: A judges the tool's technical quality, and D ranks pilots by team capacity; neither says why the business needs the pilot.
Final two: C beats B because savings claimed by a vendor are judged against an objective the group sets; the objective comes first.
Exam cue: for new technology, AI included, the first gate is the business objective it serves; value, risk and ownership follow from it.

questions.subtopic: 1B1 Enterprise risk management (ERM). Appetite change and IT thresholds
questions.question: A telecom's executive committee lowered its appetite for customer data risk, but IT's thresholds for the related KRIs still reflect the old level. What is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Keep IT's thresholds until the yearly KRI review
options.B: Have the executive committee set each IT KRI threshold
options.C: Have the IT owners accept the gap to the new appetite
options.D: Propose thresholds that match the new appetite

questions.key_concept: Enterprise appetite decisions flow down: KRI thresholds are recalibrated to a changed appetite, proposed by the practitioner.
questions.pre_read: Trace how a decision at the top reaches the indicators IT watches.
questions.correct_explanation: Appetite set at the top only works when it flows down into the limits that trigger action. Proposing KRI thresholds that match the lower appetite, for the risk owners to agree, means IT warnings fire at the level leaders now accept. Asking the executive committee to set each threshold is the runner-up: the committee sets appetite, but detailed operating thresholds are agreed below it by the risk owners, with the practitioner proposing them.

wrong_explanations.A: A change in appetite is a reason to recalibrate now. Old thresholds let exposure the committee no longer accepts pass without warning.
wrong_explanations.B: The committee sets appetite; detailed KRI thresholds are agreed below it by the risk owners, with the practitioner proposing values.
wrong_explanations.C: Accepting exposure above appetite is beyond an IT owner's authority and goes against the committee's decision to lower appetite.

tips: Eliminate: A leaves thresholds at a level leaders no longer accept, and C has owners accept exposure above the new appetite.
Final two: D beats B because leaders set appetite and risk owners agree the thresholds beneath it; the practitioner proposes them.
Exam cue: when appetite changes, expect the thresholds, KRIs and policies below it to be recalibrated; decisions at the top flow down.

questions.subtopic: 1B3 Risk profile. Combined exposure above appetite
questions.question: The risk practitioner's aggregation shows an airport operator's 12 supplier risks, each within its own tolerance, together exceed the board's appetite for supplier risk. What should the practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Escalate the combined exposure to the board
options.B: Leave the risks as reported, each within tolerance
options.C: Ask each owner to cut their risk by an equal share
options.D: Hold the finding for the next yearly profile review

questions.key_concept: Combined exposure can breach appetite while each risk is within tolerance; escalate the breach to the level that set appetite.
questions.pre_read: Separate the limits that apply to single risks from the limit that applies to the total.
questions.correct_explanation: Tolerances limit each risk, but appetite limits the total, so exposure can breach appetite while every risk stays inside its own limit. A breach of the board's appetite goes to the board, which can direct treatment, accept the position for a time or revisit the limit. Asking each owner to cut an equal share is the runner-up: owners may well act, but the practitioner would be choosing the response to a board-level breach.

wrong_explanations.B: Tolerances limit each risk; appetite limits the total. Combined exposure above appetite is a breach even when each risk sits inside its own tolerance.
wrong_explanations.C: An equal cut is a response chosen by the practitioner. The board that set the appetite decides how the breach is handled, and cuts should follow the risk.
wrong_explanations.D: A breach of appetite is a governance event. Waiting for the yearly review leaves the board unaware of exposure above its limit.

tips: Eliminate: B reads individual tolerances as if they capped the total, and D holds a breach until a scheduled review.
Final two: A beats C because a breach of the board's appetite goes to the board; the practitioner does not choose the response on its behalf.
Exam cue: aggregate exposure can breach appetite even when each risk is within tolerance; escalate to whoever set the limit that was breached.

questions.subtopic: 1A4 Policies and standards. Policy behind a business change
questions.question: A manufacturer's device policy, due for review in 18 months, predates letting staff read work email on personal phones, a risk the risk analyst rates above appetite. What is the analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Ask the policy owner to review the policy now
options.B: Keep the policy until the owner's scheduled review
options.C: Issue staff a guideline on using personal phones
options.D: Have IT publish a personal phone standard

questions.key_concept: Significant change triggers a policy review through the policy owner; the standards beneath the policy then follow it.
questions.pre_read: Notice what changed and whether the policy has kept up.
questions.correct_explanation: Policies are reviewed on schedule and after significant change, and allowing personal phones, with a risk above appetite, is such a change. Asking the policy owner to review now starts the route by which the policy is updated and approved by senior management, so the standards beneath it can follow. Having IT publish a phone standard is the runner-up: a standard may well be needed, but without the policy behind it, it lacks management's direction.

wrong_explanations.B: Scheduled reviews are a minimum. Significant change triggers a review in its own right, especially when the risk is above appetite.
wrong_explanations.C: A guideline is advisory, so staff may set it aside. It cannot bring a risk above appetite back within limits.
wrong_explanations.D: Standards carry out policy. An IT standard issued ahead of the policy lacks management's direction and may not fit the business decision.

tips: Eliminate: B waits for the schedule despite a significant change, and C answers a risk above appetite with advisory guidance.
Final two: A beats D because the policy states management's intent and comes first; the standards beneath it then follow that direction.
Exam cue: when new technology or a business decision outpaces policy, go through the policy owner for an event-driven review.

questions.subtopic: 1B5 Risk frameworks, legal, regulatory and contractual requirements. Risk handed to a provider
questions.question: A charity's HR director, who owns payroll outage risk, wants it deleted from the register now that a provider with a strong SLA runs payroll. What is the risk practitioner's BEST response?

options.A: Delete the risk and have the HR director track SLA reports
options.B: Keep the risk in the register under the HR director
options.C: Name the provider's account manager as the risk's owner
options.D: Close the risk and log the SLA in the contract register

questions.key_concept: Outsourcing and SLAs move work, not accountability: the risk stays in the register with an internal owner, re-rated for the SLA.
questions.pre_read: Ask who would feel the impact if the provider failed.
questions.correct_explanation: Outsourcing can transfer or share part of the risk, as the ISACA Glossary notes, but not the accountability: if payroll fails, the charity's staff go unpaid whatever the contract says. Keeping it in the register under the HR director keeps it owned, re-rated for the SLA and monitored. Deleting it and tracking SLA reports is the runner-up: the monitoring is right, but the remaining risk would drop out of rating and reporting.

wrong_explanations.A: Tracking SLA reports is monitoring, but deleting the risk takes the exposure that stays with the charity out of the register, so it is no longer rated or reported.
wrong_explanations.C: An outside account manager cannot own the charity's risk. Accountability for the effect on staff stays with the charity's HR director.
wrong_explanations.D: An SLA is a response that may lower the risk, not remove it. Closing the entry hides the exposure that remains with the charity.

tips: Eliminate: C gives the charity's risk to an outside party, and D closes the risk as if the SLA had removed it.
Final two: B beats A because the remaining risk must stay in the register to be rated and reported; SLA reports monitor it but do not replace the entry.
Exam cue: contracts and SLAs move work or cost, never accountability; the risk stays in the register with an internal owner.
